newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghanistan's Taleban ask U.N. to move to Kabul.
newsitem.headline: Afghanistan's Taleban ask U.N. to move to Kabul.

text.p: The purist Islamic Taleban on Thursday asked the United Nations to move its Afghan aid operation to Kabul from Pakistan, a senior Taleban official said.

The U.N. aid programme for Afghanistan has been run from the Pakistani capital of Islamabad since 1992, when it was forced to leave Kabul after heavy fighting following the fall of the communist government.
"We have asked the United Nations aid agencies to move their main offices from Islamabad to Kabul," acting Deputy Foreign Minister Sher Mohammed Abbas Stanakzai told reporters.
Stanakzai met U.N. representatives on Thursday morning. "This was not a final discussion and no decisions were taken," said Stanakzai.
A U.N. official who attended the meeting told Reuters that the programme did intend to return to Kabul, but there were a number of problems that needed to be solved.

"We were forced to shift from Kabul. When conditions allow, we will come back, we are only in Islamabad on a temporary basis," said Mohammed Saleheen, Deputy Coordinator for the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Assistance to Afghanistan.
"We are here to listen to what they say, but I have told them that the decision to come back is a political decision to be taken by the Secretary-General," said Saleheen.

"I asked them about the basic elements, for example female employees. If and when we shift to Kabul we won't only comprise men. We have female local employees and we would like to see them working," he said.

The Taleban have banned Afghan women from working except in the medical sector, although they say they are willing to allow them to go back to work if conditions laid down in their puritanical vision of Islamic law are adhered to.

"We have said to the U.N. agencies that women can work in hospitals -- doctors and nurses. Female administrative staff are not allowed to work for the time being until we can come up with new rules and regulations," said Stanakzai.

Saleheen said the Taleban had told him they agreed on such subjects as boys and girls having equal access to education, but he said he wanted to see proof. When schools reopened in Kabul last month, only boys were allowed to attend.
"We are prepared to rebuild schools, update the curriculum and provide stationery, but there has to be equality. The onus is on them." said Saleheen.
Referring to the women's issue, Saleheen said the United Nations was not trying to impose Western values on Afghanistan, but certain conditions must be met.
Stanakzai said the aim of the reqest to move to Kabul was to save money for the United Nations, and that the Taleban were ready to solve any problems that might come up.
"We have done this to save money and time. The expenditure on flights and houses in Pakistan could be saved. We have showed our readiness to solve all the problems that are pointed out by them.
"The government is ready to provide security, houses and offices. If some of the expatriates bring their familes out we will provide schools for their children," he said.
Saleheen said the United Nations intended to strengthen its presence in Kabul soon.
"We are going to strengthen our presence in the field. In the very near future we will have senior regional coordination officers in all five regions." he said.
